chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Hammad from Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Husayn (Al-Halabi) from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

He was asked about a man who has two wives, one of whom is more beloved to him than the other: Is it permissible for him to prefer one over the other? He said: Yes, he may prefer some of them over others, as long as they are not four.
And he said: If a man marries a virgin while he already has a divorcee (or mature woman), he may prefer the virgin by three days.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The meaning contained in this report regarding his preference for some over others as long as they are not four is that if a man is permitted to marry four women and have intercourse with each one in turn (one night each), it is permissible when he has two wives to assign three nights to one and one night to the other, because she is not entitled to more than one night in every four nights.

key_terms.بِكْر: Virgin (a woman who has not been married or consummated marriage before)
key_terms.ثَيِّب: Divorcee or widow (a woman who has been married before)
key_terms.لَيْلَة: Night (referring to the period of conjugal rights)
key_terms.يُفَضِّل: To prefer or give priority to

ai.seo_question: What are the rules for dividing nights between two wives in Shia Islamic law?
ai.summary: This hadith clarifies that 'equity' in polygyny refers to fairness in time allocation rather than absolute equality, allowing a husband to distribute nights unevenly (e.g., three nights to one wife and one to another) as long as the total does not exceed four. Imam al-Sadiq further specifies a jurisprudential preference for a virgin wife over a previously married one, granting her an additional three nights of preference. This ruling is central to the Shia understanding of *adl* (justice) in marital relations, distinguishing it from the Sunni view which often emphasizes equal division.
